cells.tense: You are here, holding the pen fairly while the ground settles under everyone.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what serves
cells.ask: Find one agreement with someone that you set up long ago. Let it end quietly this month, offering no explanation for why.
cells.core:
Something that looked fixed has come apart, and you're standing where it stood, still able to call it evenly. You can feel all of it and not let one feeling cast the deciding vote. No one is punished for what they felt. No one's hurt tips things on its own. That's the shape when this is working.

Keep it plain: there's probably an old agreement that was even-handed once and stopped being, without anyone announcing it. Letting it end will cost you the ease of a rule you've honoured past its usefulness — even-handed a year ago and even-handed now aren't the same thing. The people inside it have already noticed; releasing it says you noticed too, and it takes nothing to do.
cells.sheetLine: The thing that came down, you can hold it fairly.
cells.verb: feeling the whole of it and still weighing it fairly
cells.place: where something that never could stand has just come down

cells.tense: You will be bracing for whatever the clearing makes you rule on going forward.
cells.act: hold the weight as a builder holds stone
cells.ask: Whatever next wants a fair call from you, carry it a whole day and decide nothing. Hold it as weight.
cells.core:
You're weighing whether each hurt is proportionate before the hurt has finished arriving. A verdict lands while the feeling is still happening, and the one under it braces before they can speak. Even when every call is defensible, being judged that early feels like walking into a courtroom you didn't know was there.

Try holding instead. Whatever next wants a fair call, carry it one full day and decide nothing. Hold it the way a builder holds stone before knowing what wall it goes into — as weight, not as a case. Give it time to finish arriving before you rule. Once the wait is done, the call comes out shorter, and whoever it touches can hear it rather than flinch.

cells.tense: You were standing at a door that has already come down behind you.
cells.act: write the facts down in order, without feeling words
cells.ask: Choose one situation that keeps feeling unfair. Put what happened on paper in sequence, leave out how anyone felt, then read it over.
cells.core:
Something cleared, and you haven't stepped through yet. Where fairness runs between people, things sit out of balance and nobody's weighing them — least of all you. You can see it plainly and you've stopped making the call, or saying which way it should go. Nothing here needs you to be tougher. It needs one plain piece of work to start again.

Method does what nerve won't. Take one situation that feels off — a real one, not the worst — and put what happened down in sequence: this, then this, then this. Keep the page free of how anyone felt. Read it over once you're finished. You don't need to feel ready; you need the page. The call tends to arrive half made, in your own handwriting, and you can take it from there.

cells.tense: You are keeping things level between your people and telling them you stay out of it.
cells.act: listen as a student of it
cells.ask: Meet the next argument as someone new to it — hear the whole thing through before you do the move you make to even it.
cells.core:
Things between the ones near you come out even, and by your account you had nothing to do with that. But somebody shifts a word here and a weight there, and that somebody is you. The keeper tells it as a bystander, and the ones being kept level stopped buying that story a while back. They don't need to be told; the hand is visible.

Try being a beginner with it. Meet the next argument as someone new to the situation — hear all of it through before you do the move you make to even it back out. You'll catch the moment you'd normally glide past. Nothing else has to shift: that work gets seen from inside, by the one doing it.
